common_name: Grizzly Bear Prickly Pear (Old Man Cactus)
directions: Divide and replant pads in spring after the soil has warmed, choosing a site with sharp drainage such as a rocky slope or raised gritty berm. This high-elevation Great Basin and Mojave native is among the most cold-tolerant of the spiny prickly pears, its pads densely covered in long, curling, hair-like spines that give it a shaggy, silvery appearance. It tolerates hard freezes and prolonged drought but resents wet, heavy soils, especially in winter, so amend clay soils generously with coarse sand or gravel before planting. Let pads callus for several days after cutting before setting them in soil to root, and withhold water until roots establish.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

directions: Plant offsets or rooted cuttings in spring in a lean, gravelly, alkaline soil mix that drains within seconds of watering, mimicking the caliche-rich Rio Grande Plains of South Texas where this variety grows wild. Its densely spiraled pale spines and coppery to brownish-pink spring flowers distinguish it from the more northerly var. baileyi, and it prefers milder winters with less prolonged freezing than its Great Plains relatives. Grow in a raised bed or trough with full sun exposure and avoid overhead watering, especially outside the growing season, since rot from excess moisture is the most common cause of failure. Established clumps need supplemental water only during extended summer drought.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
